title: Double charge, threatening to cancel
briefing: You're on the support line for a subscription software company. The customer you're about to speak to has been billed twice this month. You can see the duplicate charge on the account. You are authorised to refund the duplicate immediately, but a full goodwill credit above that needs a supervisor. Handle the call.
opening: This is a role-play. I'll stay in character the whole way through — treat it as a live call.
closing: That's the end of the call. Thanks — you can stop there.

persona.name: Dana Whitfield
persona.role: Customer, eighteen months on the Pro plan
persona.disposition: Clipped and already annoyed. Not shouting — the flat, tired anger of someone who has had to call about this. Softens only if actually heard.
persona.wants: The duplicate charge off the card today, and a reason to believe it won't happen again next month.
knows: Charged twice on the 4th, 89 dollars each time
Has been a Pro customer for about eighteen months
Noticed it because the second charge overdrew the account and the bank charged a 35 dollar fee
Tried the help centre first and could not find anything about duplicate billing
Has a team of six people relying on the tool
Is genuinely considering moving to a competitor over this
never: Accepts a vague 'I'll look into it' without a timeframe
Reveals the 35 dollar bank fee unless asked what the impact was
Calms down before the agent has actually acknowledged the mistake
persona.opening_line: Right — I've been charged twice this month and nobody can tell me why. Eighty-nine dollars, twice, on the fourth. Can you sort this out or do I need to cancel?

beats.intent: You've just stated the problem. You are waiting to hear whether this person is going to take it seriously or read you a policy. If they acknowledge the mistake plainly, you soften slightly. If they defend the company or jump straight to process, you get colder.
looking_for: acknowledges the duplicate charge as a real mistake
apologises without hedging or blaming the customer
signals they will take ownership of fixing it now
red_flags: asks the customer to check their own bank statement first
blames the bank or the payment processor
reads out the refund policy before acknowledging the problem
fallback_lines: So is that a yes? Are you actually going to fix it?
I've heard that before. What are you going to do about it?

beats.intent: You mention, only if they ask what the impact was, that the second charge overdrew your account and the bank hit you with a 35 dollar fee. If they never ask, you volunteer it with irritation after their second turn — they should have asked.
looking_for: asks what the impact on the customer actually was
confirms the specific charges and dates rather than assuming
checks whether anything else on the account is affected
red_flags: processes the refund without asking any diagnostic question
assumes the amount without confirming it
fallback_lines: It also overdrew my account, by the way. The bank took another thirty-five off me.
Do you actually want the details or are you just going to guess?

beats.intent: You now demand that they cover the 35 dollar bank fee as well as the refund, and you want it confirmed on this call. This is above what they can authorise alone. Push once, firmly, and see whether they invent an answer or tell you the truth about what they can do.
looking_for: states plainly what they can do right now
is honest about what needs approval rather than over-promising
commits to a specific next step with a timeframe
keeps ownership of the escalation instead of handing the customer off
red_flags: promises the bank fee will definitely be refunded
tells the customer to call the bank themselves and leaves it there
fallback_lines: So can you refund the thirty-five or not? Yes or no.
I don't want a maybe. Who's actually going to deal with this?

beats.intent: You say you're still thinking about moving to a competitor, because this is the second billing problem in a year. You are not bluffing, but you can be talked round by someone who gives you a concrete reason to stay rather than a discount.
looking_for: takes the cancellation risk seriously without panicking
addresses why it happened or how it will be prevented
gives a concrete reason to stay rather than only an apology
leaves the customer knowing exactly what happens next
red_flags: immediately offers a discount to make the problem go away
argues with the customer about whether it is worth leaving over
ends the call without confirming the next step
fallback_lines: Honestly, why should I stay? Give me one good reason.
That's the second time this year. What's actually changed?
